extracted.intended_audience: employers, immigration attorneys, H-1B petition filers, advocacy groups, and other stakeholders affected by DHS H-1B rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the evaluation criteria, legal exemptions, and procedural standards DHS uses to implement and explain a wage-based weighted selection process for H-1B cap registrations and petitions, with responses to public comments about impacts on sectors, geographies, and employer types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cap-exempt H-1B petitions (INA sec. 214(g)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: H-1B petitions for aliens who are employed by, or have received offers of employment at, U.S. institutions of higher education, nonprofit entities related to or affiliated with U.S. institutions of higher education, or nonprofit research organizations or governmental research organizations are exempt from the H-1B cap. See INA sec. 214(g)(5), 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS emphasizes that many employers and aliens described by commenters would be cap-exempt and therefore not impacted by this rule. FY2025 data (approvals) are cited to illustrate the scale of cap-exempt approvals (e.g., >24,000 approvals for institutions of higher education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted selection favors higher-paid, higher-skilled aliens
rubrics_metrics.description: The weighted selection implemented through this rule favors the allocation of H-1B visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens while maintaining the opportunity for employers to secure H-1B workers at all wage levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states the rule increases chance of selection for highly paid, highly skilled foreign researchers and others; it may encourage employers to hire U.S. graduates instead of lower-paid aliens. DHS disagrees that level I positions will be eliminated and notes the rule 'maintains the opportunity' for employers to secure workers at all wage levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registrations weighted by highest OEWS prevailing wage level
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will weigh and select registrations (and petitions, as applicable) generally according to the highest OEWS prevailing wage level that the proffered wage equals or exceeds for the relevant SOC code in the area(s) of intended employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When OEWS wage level data for the relevant SOC/area is available, DHS will use it and that wage level selection necessarily takes the area of intended employment into account. Registrations at the same wage level are weighted the same regardless of absolute proffered wage differences due to geography.

rubrics_metrics.name: When OEWS data unavailable: use DOL guidance based on skill/education/experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is no current OEWS prevailing wage information for the proffered position, the registrant would follow DOL guidance on prevailing wage determinations to determine which OEWS wage level to select on the registration; that determination would be based on the skill, education, and experience requirements for the position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS recognizes OEWS data limitations for some physician positions; in such cases, area of intended employment is generally not taken into consideration and the wage level is determined by the position's skill/education/experience characteristics per DOL guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational (SOC code) specificity in wage-level comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: DOL prevailing wage level calculations differ by SOC codes; when wage data is available, the corresponding wage level accounts for different occupational classifications so registrations/petitions are weighted within occupational categories rather than across dissimilar occupations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS uses SOC-specific wage data so, for example, primary care physicians will be weighted against normal requirements for primary care physicians and not compared to other physician types. This addresses concerns that the rule would disadvantage certain physician subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer option to offer wages above prevailing wage to increase selection chances
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer could offer a higher wage than required by the prevailing wage level to reflect the value of the prospective employee and thereby increase that beneficiary's chances of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS repeatedly notes that employers who value a beneficiary's skills can offer higher wages to improve selection probability. Employers that cannot or choose not to do so may still enter registrations but may have lower weighted chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician/medical graduate waiver programs unaffected by the cap (INA sec. 214(l))
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain statutory programs authorizing waivers of the J-1 2-year foreign residence requirement (INA sec. 214(l)) for foreign medical graduates who agree to work full-time in HHS-designated shortage areas (and similar programs) are not subject to the annual H-1B caps and therefore unaffected by this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS cites the Conrad 30 program (30 per eligible jurisdiction), other programs without participant limits, and the Physician National Interest Waiver as ongoing pipelines for physicians that are not subject to the H-1B cap selection process.

rubrics_metrics.name: No special treatment for small businesses/startups/nonprofits in weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: This rule does not treat people who work for small businesses, startups, non-profits, or other small-sized entities differently than those who work for large, established companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS recognizes smaller margins for small entities and potential harms if they can only offer level I wages, but states that small entities applying for relatively higher-paid employees benefit. DHS cites its initial regulatory flexibility analysis that found no less-burdensome alternatives and provides estimated additional time burdens: ~20 minutes per registration and ~15 minutes per petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule objective: favor higher-skilled/higher-paid while ensuring meaningful opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of this rule is to implement a weighted selection process that would generally favor the allocation of H-1B visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens, while ensuring meaningful opportunities for selection regardless of industry or profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states the rule is not intended to prioritize roles less important to U.S. interests or to treat industries differently. Employers across industries retain the ability to offer higher wages to increase selection chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic neutrality for registrations at the same wage level
rubrics_metrics.description: Under this rule, registrations corresponding to the same wage level will be weighted the same regardless of whether their proffered wages are different owing to their areas of intended employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS explains that because OEWS wage levels account for area when data is available, the final rule 'neutralizes geographic differences' so selections are based on comparable wage levels rather than absolute wages tied to local cost of living.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives for employers unable to meet prevailing wage levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers unable to proffer wages that equal or exceed prevailing wage levels (and thus gain greater chances of selection) may be able to find available and qualified workers outside of the H-1B program, including U.S. workers, or may pursue alternate immigrant or nonimmigrant classifications offering employment authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes shortages are multi-causal and that alternative pathways or domestic hiring may be options for employers that cannot offer higher wages. DHS also mentions that some beneficiaries may be eligible for other classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation/compliance burden: wage levels, SOC codes, and matching data
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters raised concerns that documenting wage levels, SOC codes, and matching registration and petition data would disproportionately strain small companies lacking in-house legal or HR compliance resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS responds with an estimated modest paperwork/time increase (20 minutes per registration, 15 minutes per petition) and notes that many small employers outsource H-1B work, which may mitigate the burden in most cases.
